Over this course you will learn how to confirm exactly what our clients owe to the providers, insurers and other third parties who treated or covered them. This work sits right at the end of a personal injury case, just before the money goes out, so accuracy here protects the client, the firm and you. Let's begin with the outline for today.

Here is our path for today. We start with an introduction and overview, so everyone shares the same definitions. Then we look at the types of liens a specialist may run into. Next comes the framework we follow, and finally we cover how to identify potential medical liens in a file. Let's start with the overview. Before we touch any process or software, we need a clear picture of what lien balance verification is, who the lienholders are, and why getting the balance right matters so much to the client and to the firm. Everything later in the training rests on these basics.

This is the definition to remember. Lien balance verification is the process of confirming the accurate amount of money owed to healthcare providers, insurers or other third parties for services provided to someone in a personal injury case. The key word is accurate. We are not guessing or estimating. We confirm the real figure with the party that is owed, because that figure comes straight out of the client's settlement.

So what is a lien in our world? It is a claim by a healthcare provider, insurer or other third party that provided services or coverage to the injured client. Lienholders include hospitals, doctors and insurance companies, and that includes government programs like Medicare and Medicaid. They have a right to be reimbursed for what they spent treating or covering our client. As a Closing Specialist, you will deal with every one of these.

Here is how a lien actually works. It is a legal mechanism that makes sure providers are paid from the settlement or judgment the client receives. In effect, the settlement becomes the asset the lien is placed against. Once the case settles, the lienholders are paid from those funds first, and only then is the remaining amount disbursed to the client. That order is why verified balances must be ready before disbursement.

Why does this matter to the client? Settling liens properly reduces the client's risk of building up bad credit from unpaid medical bills. It also means that once they receive compensation, all their medical expenses are covered. Think about a client who gets their check and then months later receives a collection notice. That is exactly what careful verification prevents, and it is something the client will remember about our firm.

And what is in it for the firm? When we resolve liens well, it shows thoroughness and real care for the client's financial well-being. Clients value getting their maximum net settlement quickly. That builds trust, and trust is what enhances the firm's reputation and brings referrals. So your accuracy and speed on lien verification directly shape how clients feel about the whole case, not just the closing.

Now let's move to the types of liens. Not every lien comes from a doctor or hospital, and each type is handled a little differently. Knowing which kind you are looking at is the first step to verifying it correctly.

A specialist may encounter several types of liens: medical liens, attorney liens, pre-settlement liens, worker's compensation liens and miscellaneous liens. Medical liens will be most of your daily work, but the others can show up on the same file. A common mistake is focusing only on medical bills and missing, say, a pre-settlement funding lien. We will look at each type next, so keep this list in mind.

Medical liens are the ones you will see most. They are claims placed by healthcare providers so they are compensated for the medical services they gave the client after the accident. These liens are typically attached to whatever settlement the client receives. In practice, that means every treating provider in the file is a possible lienholder, and each one needs its balance confirmed before we can close the case.

Attorney liens are claims made by an attorney for unpaid legal services. They make sure that attorney is paid for the work done on the client's case, even before the client receives the settlement. You may see this when a client changed firms partway through the case. The earlier attorney's claim still has to be accounted for, so watch the file history for prior representation.

Pre-settlement liens come from funding companies. These companies give clients financial help, loans or advances, while the case is still pending, expecting to be repaid once the settlement is reached. Clients sometimes forget to mention these advances, or do not think of them as debts. So it is worth asking the client directly whether they took any funding while the case was open.

A worker's compensation lien is a claim by an insurance provider to recover the cost of benefits it paid to an injured employee, things like medical expenses and lost wages. If that worker then receives compensation from a third-party lawsuit, the insurer may place a lien for reimbursement. So whenever the injury happened on the job, flag the file for a possible workers' comp lien.

Miscellaneous liens cover any other claims against the settlement that do not fit the usual categories of medical, attorney or pre-settlement liens. Examples on the slide are unpaid debts, child support, and government claims such as Medicare or Medicaid. These are easy to miss because they do not come from treatment, so read the whole file and any notices carefully.

Next, the purpose. Why do we spend so much care verifying lien balances instead of just paying whatever number is on the bill? The next four slides give the answers: accurate recovery, preventing overpayment, legal compliance and maximizing client recovery.

The first purpose is accurate financial recovery. Verifying lien balances correctly gives us financial precision, keeps us within legal standards, and builds trust in the subrogation and settlement process. Everyone involved, the client, the providers and the insurers, needs to be able to rely on our numbers. One wrong balance can undermine confidence in the entire closing statement.

The second purpose is preventing overpayment. If we pay a lien without verifying the balance, we may pay a provider or another party in the subrogation process more than they are actually owed. Every overpaid dollar comes out of the client's pocket, and getting it back afterwards is slow and difficult. Verification before payment is far easier than recovery after it.

The third purpose is legal compliance. Verification makes sure that every provider, insurance company and third party with a right to repayment from the settlement funds is accounted for. Confirming these obligations protects the injured client, and the firm as their legal representative, from lawsuits or collection actions later. Missing a valid lien is not just a mistake, it can become a legal problem.

The fourth purpose is maximizing client recovery. Once lien balances are verified, the attorneys can negotiate reductions where they apply. That is how the client ends up with the most money possible after every obligation is settled. You cannot negotiate a number you have not confirmed, so verification is the foundation for every reduction request that follows.

The last purpose is preventing settlement delays. Finalizing a settlement often depends on every lien being resolved. If a balance is wrong or unconfirmed, the funds sit in trust while we sort it out, and the client waits. Accurate verification up front means everyone receives the correct amount and the money moves on time. Delays are one of the most common client complaints, and this is how we avoid them.

Now let's look at the workflow. We will see where lien work sits in the life of a case, from the date of loss through disbursement, and then the specific steps a specialist follows when verifying liens. Keep the five stages of a case in mind as we go.

Here is the life of a case, starting from the date of loss, the day of the accident. From there the case is set up, the client goes through treatment, the case settles, liens are negotiated, and finally funds are disbursed. Our work in lien verification sits between settlement and disbursement, but it depends on everything recorded earlier, especially the treatment history and the date of loss itself.

This diagram shows the steps inside lien work. They include collecting coverage information, confirming treatments, verifying the last day of treatment, verifying lien balances, requesting final lien balances, and lien negotiation. Each step feeds the next. For example, you cannot request a final balance until you know treatment has ended. We will go through these steps in detail as the training continues, so use this as your map.

These are the non-negotiables, the four things that must happen on every file without exception. First, accurately identify and compile the liens. Second, verify them. Third, resolve any discrepancies you find. Fourth, conduct an accurate final review before anything is paid. Skipping any one of these is how overpayments, missed liens and delays happen. If you are short on time, these four still get done.

Let's turn to the framework for medical liens. This is the simple four-stage life cycle of a medical lien, from treatment to payment. Once you see the cycle, you will know where any lien in a file currently stands. Each stage gets its own slide.

Stage one is medical treatment. After the injury, the client receives care. That care is often covered by health insurance, or the providers agree to delay payment until the personal injury case is resolved. Either way, someone has paid or is waiting to be paid, and that is where the lien begins. Knowing which of the two applies tells you who to contact later.

Stage two is the lien being established. The healthcare providers or insurers file a lien against the future settlement, so they are repaid once the client receives compensation for the injury. At this point the lien is a claim on money that does not exist yet. Our job is to make sure every one of these claims is on our list.

Stage three is case settlement. Once the personal injury case reaches a resolution, the settlement or court award is granted. Now there is a real sum of money that the liens attach to. This is the moment when verified balances become urgent, because the client is waiting for their share and lienholders are waiting for theirs.

Stage four is lien payment. Before the client receives their portion of the settlement, the lienholders must be reimbursed for the medical expenses or services they covered. That order is fixed. The client is paid last, which is exactly why accurate, verified balances matter: every dollar we get right on the liens is a dollar the client can count on.

The final stage is client disbursement. After all liens are paid, the remaining funds from the settlement go to the client. This is the moment the client has been waiting for since the accident. If the earlier stages were done carefully, this step is simple and on time. If a lien was missed or misstated, this is where the problem surfaces, often with the client already expecting their check.

Here is the whole framework in one view. Medical treatment and services are provided, the lien is established, the case settles, the liens are paid, and then the client's share is disbursed. Five stages, always in this order. When you open any file, ask yourself which stage it is in. That tells you what has already happened and what needs to happen next.

Let's see how it works with real numbers. We will walk through a sample scenario and the settlement calculation, so you can see exactly how liens and fees come out of a settlement before the client's net is reached. Have a pen ready and follow along.

Let's do the math. The client's case settled for twenty-five thousand dollars. Medical bills owed are ten thousand, miscellaneous liens are one thousand, and attorney's fees are two thousand. Take all three from the settlement and the net proceeds for the client are twelve thousand dollars. Try it yourself: twenty-five thousand minus thirteen thousand. Notice how much the medical bills drive the result, which is why verifying them matters.

Here is the settlement calculation step by step. Start with the total settlement amount. Subtract medical bills and expenses, the costs not covered under liens, such as out-of-pocket costs the client pays directly. Subtract liens, the amounts owed to lienholders like medical providers or financing companies. Then subtract attorney's fees, typically a percentage of the total settlement. What remains is the client's net, and every figure in it should be verified, not estimated.

This picture pulls the calculation together. Start with the settlement. Subtract medical bills and expenses, subtract liens, and subtract attorney's fees. What is left is the total net disbursement to the client. Keep this picture in your head whenever you prepare a net sheet. If any one of those three boxes is wrong, the client's number at the bottom is wrong too.

Now let's talk about significance. Liens are not only something we pay off at the end. They also do real good for clients during the case, and understanding that helps you speak with providers and clients with the right attitude.

First, liens give clients access to immediate medical treatment. Because of liens, clients can get timely care for their injuries without paying upfront. That lets them focus on recovering instead of worrying about how to pay for treatment. Remember this when you talk to providers. They took a risk by treating on a lien, and that is worth acknowledging in every conversation.

Second, liens ease the financial burden. Treatment without immediate cost reduces the strain that usually comes with a medical emergency. That is especially important for clients who have no health insurance or not enough savings to pay medical expenses upfront. For many of our clients, a lien is the only reason they were able to get treated at all.

Third, liens can improve health outcomes. Prompt care can prevent complications, shorten recovery time and improve the overall prognosis. That benefits the client, and it also benefits the insurance providers involved. So the lien system, when it works well, is good for everyone. Our part is to close it out accurately so providers keep trusting the process.

To sum up significance: liens can look like a burden at first, especially when a client sees how much comes out of their settlement. But liens are what gave them access to care, reduced their financial stress and helped their health, all without upfront out-of-pocket costs. When you explain this to clients, it helps them see medical liens with a more positive perspective, and conversations go more smoothly.

Now we move into the mainstream of our work, the actual lien balance verification process. From here on, we go step by step through what you do on a file, starting with when the process begins. This is the heart of your daily work.

Here is where we start. The lien balance verification process is initiated under the lien negotiation phase. In other words, once the case has reached the point of negotiating liens, verifying the balances is the first thing we do. You cannot negotiate a lien until you know exactly what is owed, so verification always comes first within that phase.

This slide shows the sequence. Settlement comes first, then lien verification, then lien negotiation. Verification sits right after the settlement and right before negotiation. That placement matters. If you skip verification and go straight to negotiating, you may be negotiating against the wrong number, and any reduction you win could still leave the client overpaying.

Step one is collecting coverage data. Start by making sure you have all the relevant medical records, including treatment details, procedures and related bills for the injury. The documentation should be comprehensive. A missing record often means a missing provider, and a missing provider means a lien that could surface after the client has been paid. Check the file against the treatment history.

Next, collect information about the client's health insurance plan. Pay particular attention to the coverage type, the deductibles and the copayments, because these affect who paid what. If you cannot find this information easily in the file, reach out to the insurance provider or to the client directly. Do not guess at coverage. A wrong assumption here carries through every balance that follows.

Once you have the medical records and the coverage information, you can start identifying any potential liens related to the client's medical treatment. Each provider who treated the client and each insurer that paid is a possible lienholder. This is where the list of liens for the file begins to take shape, and the next step is to confirm the details with each of them.

Step two is obtaining lien details. Reach out to the healthcare providers and insurers and request lien information. You need accurate and up-to-date balances, not old figures from the intake file. That is why every facility's and insurer's contact details should always be verified and kept updated in your CMS. A wrong fax number or address can cost days on a closing.

Be ready for this. Providers may not share information with you over the phone right away. To get what you need, they might ask for more documentation, such as a Release of Information form signed by the client, in compliance with HIPAA. This is normal and it protects the client's privacy. Having the signed form ready before you call saves a lot of back and forth.

So what is a Release of Information form? It is a legal document that allows a third party, such as a healthcare provider or insurance company, to share personal information or records. In personal injury cases, we use it to obtain medical records and billing statements for claims processing, lien management and settlement negotiations. Make sure the one in the file is signed and current before you rely on it.

When you prepare the ROI, four things must be accurate: the provider's information, the date of service, the client's index information, and the client's signature. If any of these is wrong or missing, the provider can reject the form, and you lose days waiting for a corrected one. Take a moment to check each item against the file before the form goes out.

Send the balance verification request form and the ROI form together, by email or by fax, whichever the provider prefers. Sending them together means the provider has everything needed to answer in one go. Ask which method they prefer when you call, and note it in the file so the next request goes the right way the first time.

When a provider confirms that a lien exists, ask whether a third-party handler manages the balances. Some providers hand their lien accounts to outside companies. If so, get the handler's name and contact information. Otherwise you may send your request to the provider and wait, while the people who actually hold the balance never see it.

Once you have spoken with the representative and know who handles the balance and how they want to receive requests, submit the balance verification request by email or fax to confirm the client's balance. The phone call sets things up. The written request is what produces the confirmed figure we rely on, so always follow the call with the request.

Create the balance verification form using the firm's CRM or CMS. If that option is not available, you may need to draft the form from scratch. It also helps to ask for copies of previously sent forms to use as references. Using the system whenever you can keeps the format consistent and makes sure the request is saved with the case.

Step three is follow up. Keep track of the progress of every request you send so you always know where your case stands. A request that goes out and is never chased is one of the most common reasons a closing stalls. Set yourself reminders, and when a provider has not answered, follow up rather than waiting.

Regular communication with lienholders does more than chase answers. It lets you assess the costs as they build up and compare them against the policy limits of the party managing the liability. If the liens are approaching or exceeding those limits, the attorney needs to know early, because it affects settlement and any reductions we request.

Always get confirmation for every request you send, every document you receive and any communication with lienholders. Then save it in your CMS or drives for future reference. If a lienholder later disputes what was agreed or when a request was sent, that saved confirmation is your proof. If it is not documented, assume it did not happen.

That brings us to the end of Day 1. We covered what lien balance verification is, the types of liens, the purpose and framework, the math, and the first three steps of the process. Take a moment to note your questions, and we will pick up from here next session.
